problem: Existing embodied simulators rely on hand-made scenes or procedural templates, and LLM-based 3D generators only produce static scenes without verifiable tasks, standard learning interfaces, or feedback from the learning agent.
motivation: Digital agents benefit from abundant, automatically generated interactive sandboxes, while embodied agents lack diverse, physically grounded, deployable environments. A generator that self-improves and adapts to the learner's frontier could turn environment generation into an adaptive curriculum.
key_idea: A tool/skill-augmented coding agent (SimCoder) writes engine-level UE5 code to build verified, Gym-exportable environments, self-evolves its tool/skill library from verifier feedback, and co-evolves with an embodied agent via performance-gated difficulty curricula.
insight: The ablation shows structured MCP tools are a hard prerequisite (vanilla agent 0.16 -> 0.45 with tools), verification adds +0.10, and self-evolution adds the largest further gain (+0.21) by accumulating reusable strategies. Scene diversity (1 to 30 environments at a fixed 200-episode budget) drives generalization, and adaptive difficulty beats fixed difficulty (90% vs 72% on SimWorld-MMNav) because the fixed-level agent saturates midway.
method: SimCoder with MCP tools: an LLM coding agent (run in Claude Code) calls 14 primitive MCP tools (spawn/delete/transform actors, setup_environment, list_assets, screenshot, verify_scene, collision and support checks) plus a Python escape hatch. Useful patterns are promoted to named wrapper tools.

Skill library: Markdown skills describing how to compose tools (5 built-in: building-placement, city-layout, street-furniture, weather-and-mood, screenshot-tour). Skills are retrieved at the start of each episode, and new ones are authored through self-evolution.

Verification loop: a rule-based verifier (AABB collisions, vertical support, in-bounds) runs on every actor-modifying call. A VLM verifier gets 6 multi-view screenshots and returns PASS/NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT/FAIL with suggestions, for up to 3 rounds; feedback re-enters as the next observation.
Self-evolution: on recurring verifier failures, SimCoder generalizes the failure to a class and writes a new tool or skill to the registry for all later runs.

Task generation and Gym compilation: NavMesh yields solvable PointNav/ObjectNav episodes (start-goal sampled, A* shortest path, 3-20 m filter). Each scene is exported as a Gymnasium env with reset()/step(), returning RGB-D, pose and reward.
Embodied agent memory: a training-free 3-level memory (step, trajectory, task) extending Generative Agents and ExpeL, retrieved at inference for Qwen3.5 agents.

Co-evolution curriculum: 8 difficulty levels (path length, heading offset, obstacle density); the agent appends failure-derived prioritized rules (structured GEPA variant, cap 30); SimCoder advances the level when rolling SR exceeds a level threshold (0.80 down to 0.45).

setting.backbone: SimCoder: Claude Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 / Qwen3.5-27B / Qwen3.5-9B (frozen, via Claude Code); embodied agent: Qwen3.5-2B/9B/27B (frozen LLM + in-context memory/rules)
setting.training_data: No weight training; embodied agents learn in-context from 1.2K generated training episodes per task (CS2) or 500 episodes over 25 epochs (CS3) in SimCoder-generated UE5 environments
setting.observation: RGB 224x224 plus bearing and geodesic distance to goal and step count (RGB-D available in the Gym interface)
setting.action_space: discrete: move_forward 0.25 m, turn_left 15°, turn_right 15°, stop (40-step episode limit in CS2)
setting.privileged: none at test time (bearing and distance to goal are given as observations; training episodes use NavMesh geodesic references)

results: Opus 4.6 generates the best scenes (avg 0.77/0.79/0.75 for S1/S2/S3). Agents with memory trained in generated environments improve on held-out envs (e.g. Qwen3.5-9B ObjectNav SR 0.00 -> 14.62) and transfer to SimWorld-MMNav. Co-evolution reaches 90% SR on SimWorld-MMNav vs 72% fixed-difficulty and 50% untrained.
limitations: Quality is bounded by the coding agent's spatial reasoning; fine-grained multi-object arrangement can fail, and smaller Qwen models do poorly.

Navigation-only case studies with a simple performance-gated curriculum, evaluated on a single 9B model and few scenes (9 generation scenes); co-evolution results come from one figure without variance.
Agent 'training' is in-context memory or rules rather than gradient RL; the platform was not shown with PPO.
